bio.en: Brian Tolkin is Head of Product and Design at Opendoor, previously an early Uber employee (#100) who started in operations, led uberPOOL's launch, and created Uber's product-operations function.
bio.zh: Brian Tolkin 是 Opendoor 产品与设计负责人，此前是 Uber 早期员工（第 100 号），从运营起步，领导了 uberPOOL 的发布，并创立了 Uber 的产品运营职能。

summary.en: Brian shares lessons on building products with a heavy operational component, arguing that ops experience gives a deep understanding of how the business actually works. He covers how to run great product reviews, how Opendoor applies the Jobs-to-be-Done framework, and the story of Zillow competing with then partnering Opendoor. The conversation is full of stories from the early days of Uber and Opendoor on scaling operationally-heavy tech companies.
summary.zh: Brian 分享了打造“强运营属性”产品的经验，认为运营经历让人深刻理解业务实际如何运转。他讲述了如何做好产品评审、Opendoor 如何应用“待办任务”框架，以及 Zillow 先竞争后合作的故事。对话充满了 Uber 与 Opendoor 早期扩展“重运营”科技公司的故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've worked at two businesses that have done incredibly well combining product in ops.
turns.zh: 你待过两家把产品和运营结合得特别好的公司。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Uber always has this mentality and Opendoor does two of the product operations, twin turbine jet plane where you can fly the plane on one engine for a little bit if you need to, but it's operating most efficiently and effectively if both are working together.
turns.zh: Uber一直有这种心态，Opendoor也是——把它想成双涡轮喷气飞机，必要时你可以靠一台发动机飞一阵，但两台一起转，才是最有效率、最有效果的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What has having been in ops done to make you a better product leader?
turns.zh: 做过运营，怎么让你成了一个更好的产品负责人？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Gave a really deep understanding of how the business actually works. It's a pretty good foundation for them going on to say, okay, what do we actually want to build in a more scalable technology way.
turns.zh: 它让我极深地理解了这门生意到底是怎么运转的。这给后面说'好，那我们到底想用更可规模化的技术去建什么'打下了很好的底。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else I've heard that you're very good at is staying very calm under pressure.
turns.zh: 我还听说你另一项强项是：在压力下特别能保持冷静。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I've slept on the floor in China before launching uberPOOL, and when you reflect the stress onto your teams, everybody tenses out. It counterintuitively doesn't produce better outcomes.
turns.zh: 在uberPOOL中国上线前，我睡过中国办公室的地板。当你把压力反射给团队，所有人都会绷紧。反直觉的是，这并不会带来更好的结果。

Also, how to run great product reviews, how he implements the jobs to be done, framework and Opendoor's successfully. (00:01:32): The story behind Zillow trying to compete with Opendoor failing and then partnering instead. Plus a ton of great stories from the early days of Uber and Opendoor, and so much more. turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I want to spend a bunch of time talking about product and ops. You started your career in operations. At Uber you actually started on the ops team and you moved into product. You've also worked at both Uber and at Opendoor, which have both huge operational components. I think it's really rare that people, one, see a company scale to the heights of Uber and Opendoor with such a heavy operational component that are still tech companies and also it's really where someone starts an ops and then moves into product and ends up where you are, where your chief product officer, really successful company. So I have a bunch of questions here. Maybe the first is just what has having been in ops done to make you a better product leader? How does that change the way that you operate as a product leader?
turns.zh: 好，我想花大把时间聊产品和运营。你是做运营起家的。在Uber你从运营团队开始，后来转到产品。你还在Uber和Opendoor都干过，这两家都有极重的运营成分。我觉得很罕见的一点：第一，能有一家公司带着这么重的运营成分、还能 scaling 到Uber和Opendoor这种高度、同时还是科技公司；第二，有人从运营起步、转去做产品、最后成了你——一家很成功公司的首席产品官。所以我有好多问题。第一个也许是：做过运营，怎么让你成了更好的产品负责人？它怎么改变了你作为产品负责人的运作方式？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Starting on the operations side gave a really deep understanding of how the business actually works. You are truly operating it day in and day out and the success of the city is in large part driven by the inputs that you are putting into it every single day on the ground and whether or not there was rain that weekend, which was a nice driver of metrics, but talking to customers every single day like one-on-one onboarding drivers responding to support tickets, there's no centralized support team, there was no closer to the customer, right? And so I think that foundation actually for really understanding what moves the business and being super close to the customer actually is a pretty good foundation for them going on to say, okay, what do we actually want to build in a more scalable technology way?
turns.zh: 从运营侧起步，让我极深地理解了这门生意到底怎么运转。你是日复一日真在 operate 它，一个城市的成败，很大程度上取决于你每天在地面上投进去的那些输入——比如周末下没下雨，那可是个挺好用的指标驱动因素；但更重要的是每天跟客户一对一聊：给司机做 onboarding、回支持工单，那时根本没有集中的支持团队，没有人比运营更贴近客户，对吧？所以我觉得，这个'真正懂什么在驱动业务、又超级贴近客户'的底子，对后面说'好，我们到底想用更可规模化的技术建什么'，是个很好的基础。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question and I think Uber always had this mentality and OpenDoor does too of like a twin turbine jet plane where you can fly the plane on one engine for a little bit if you need to, but it's operating most efficiently and effectively if both are working together, and I think that's really true, right? The reality is operations teams, local teams, can iterate faster, can scale talking to customers really much more efficiently, have great qualitative insights, and so if it's seen more as a harmony instead of a competition, I think that's really, really helpful where it's like, okay, how do we get the insights that are happening day in and day out in the field, on the ground, whatever that may be, and help us build better products because of that, right? (00:07:50): Like a PM sitting in San Francisco can't be in Opendoor's case 50 markets, walking houses every single day in Uber's case, whatever, a thousand cities understanding the nuances of safety in South America and it's just not possible, but what you can do is foster a really good relationship and a really good feedback loop of how people who do deeply understand those things can help give insights. Now is actually the birth of product operations was that insight as well.
turns.zh: 好问题。我觉得Uber一直有这种心态，Opendoor也是——像双涡轮喷气飞机，必要时你能靠一台发动机飞一阵，但两台一起转才最有效率、最有效果，对吧？现实是，运营团队、本地团队，能迭代得更快，能极其高效地跟客户聊、有极好的定性洞察。所以如果把它看成'和声'而不是'竞争'，那就特别有帮助——就像说：好，我们怎么把前线、地面上每天发生的洞察弄出来，用它们帮我们建更好的产品？（00:07:50）比如一个PM坐在旧金山，不可能像Opendoor那样同时在50个市场、每天去walk房子；也不可能像Uber那样在一千个城市里理解南美安全的细微差别，根本不可能。但你能做的是：培养一种很好的关系、一个很好的反馈环——让那些真正深懂这些事的人，能把洞察给出来。而产品运营的诞生，其实正是来自这个洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you say more on that?
turns.zh: 能再展开讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, sure. So, sorry, I should probably define what product operations was. At Uber it was basically this notion that we had centralized, this was later in my career at Uber, but we had a centralized product team building stuff mostly in San Francisco, not strictly through the Ross, but at this point around the world, but mostly in San Francisco and then we had a very globally distributed operations team, and there was a bidirectional feedback loop that wasn't super strong and that feedback loop was basically when the EPD teams in San Francisco built new features, how do we effectively put it in global markets and then how do we effectively get input from global markets to better build features. And so one solution to that problem, our solution at the time was to start up a new function called product operations who had accountability and reported into operations but physically sat with and operated much like a member of the product team to help solve that.
turns.zh: 好，当然。先抱歉，我大概该先定义一下产品运营是什么。在Uber，那基本是这个概念：我们当时有个集中的产品团队，主要在旧金山建东西——严格说不完全通过Ross，但那会儿已经全球铺开了，不过主要在旧金山；同时我们有个高度全球分布的运营团队。两者之间有个双向反馈环，但不够强。那个环基本就是：旧金山那边的EPD团队建了新功能，怎么有效地铺到全球市场；以及怎么有效地从全球市场拿到输入、去把功能建得更好。所以当时的一个解法是：新开一个叫'产品运营'的职能，它对运营负责汇报，但物理上坐在产品团队里、运作起来也像个产品团队成员，来帮忙解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that maybe the first time there's a... Did you invent product operations as a function?
turns.zh: 这算不算第一次有人把'产品运营'当成一个职能？是你发明的吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I don't think so because at the time, I believe Google had a function, I can't remember what Google called it was something slightly different, but I met with a few folks who had been in similar type roles at Google and a couple other places, so I don't take credit for certainly for inventing IT and other people have actually dabbled in this model at Uber before me there was just a formalization of it and our actual building out of the organization, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我不觉得是我发明的，因为当时我记得Google好像有个类似职能，叫什么我忘了，略有不同，但我见过几个在Google和其他一两家干过类似角色的人。所以我绝对不敢抢'发明'这个功劳，而且在我之前Uber里也有人试过这个模式，我们只是把它正式化了、真正把组织建了起来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did none of that. Sounds like you basically helped make it a thing. I know you're being very modest, I think. Coming back to your point about decentralized operations teams, something I've read is that search pricing came out of one GM and a market just testing, emailing all the drivers, hey, we're going to give you extra if you drive on Saturday night. Is that true?
turns.zh: 完全没有。听起来你基本就是把它变成了一个真东西。我知道你很谦虚。回到你说的去中心化运营团队，我读到过一种说法：动态定价（surge pricing）最早是一个GM在某个市场自己试出来的——给所有司机发邮件：'周六晚上开车我们给你加钱。'是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: That would've been probably a little bit before my time, but that being said, one thing that is true is that surge pricing for actually quite sometimes all of 2012, certainly 2013 probably, I don't know when we necessarily switched, was very much a human in the loop system or a very manual system where GMs in every city would control basically the parameters in which surge would operate and so much of the time that would need, for example, Monday through Friday, there would be no search, it couldn't flip on, and then Friday nights and Saturday nights it would flip on from whatever you set, 7:00 PM to 3:00 AM and the cap was X, whatever the cap was. And then within those parameters the algorithm would optimize for what the price was. But yeah, GMs controlled whether it was on or off and what geographies were surging.
turns.zh: 那大概在我来之前一点点。但有一点是真的：surge pricing在相当长时间里——整个2012年、肯定还有2013年，我不知道我们到底哪天切的——基本是个'人在回路'的系统，或者说很手工的系统。每个城市的GM控制着surge生效的参数。很多时候，比如周一到周五根本不会开surge，开不了；然后周五、周六晚上，从你设的晚上7点到凌晨3点它会打开，上限是X。在这些参数之内，算法再去优化价格。但没错，GM控制着开还是关、以及哪些区域在surge。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I didn't know that. Was that out of we believe we are better than the algorithms or we just don't have time to make them amazing yet, so we're just going to help them along?
turns.zh: 哇，我不知道这个。这是因为我们觉得自己比算法强，还是单纯没时间把算法做到位，所以先帮一把？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, I think it was probably a function of a bunch of stuff, one of which is like, hey, this is a fairly new concept and it's powerful and dangerous and so let's make sure we understand what's happening. The second is this belief that local city teams know their cities best and so you might know that an event is happening, a baseball game gets out and it's like, oh, I know that this baseball game's going to get out at 10:00 PM so I'm going to set surge at 9:45 and the algorithm may not be able to pick that up. And then the third is the technical constraint of nowadays clearly it's all automated, but it's really hard to build a fully dynamic, always on geospatially aware pricing system and not just a little bit of time.
turns.zh: 我觉得可能是好几件事的合力。其一：嘿，这是个挺新、又强又危险的概念，所以咱们先确保搞懂发生了什么。其二是个信念——本地城市团队最懂自己的城市。你可能知道有个活动、一场棒球赛要散场，你就会想'哦我知道这场10点散，所以9点45我把surge设上'，算法未必抓得到这个。其三是技术限制：今天当然全自动了，但在当时，建一个完全动态、永远在线、能感知地理位置的定价系统，真的很难，不是一点时间就能搞定的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. I feel like you're full of wild stories from your time at Uber. Is there one that comes to mind of just, I think you helped scale in China, uberPOOL?
turns.zh: 有道理。我觉得你Uber时期有一肚子疯狂故事。有没有哪个一下子冒出来的？我记得你好像帮忙在中国 scaling 了uberPOOL？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe that's the one. I don't know. Can you share wild story from early Uber days?
turns.zh: 也许就是那个。我不知道。能分享个Uber早期wild story吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, so in the early days of Uber, one fun story is obviously UberX is a random mainstream product but has a funny, silly name, UberX. This product in the early days was going to be all hybrid and had a bunch of different potential names. I was not personally driving this, this was someone else on the operations team, but they built the model for what this product could be and there's no name for it yet, so it was going to be a placeholder. So what do you put in some placeholder? X. So UberX and then the company was moving quickly enough, the product got the green light, it launched, and here we are, I don't know, 12 years later, 11 years later, whatever it is and UberX is the name that stuck.
turns.zh: 好。Uber早期有个好玩的事：UberX现在是个主流产品，但名字很傻很随意。这个产品早期本来要做成全混动，有一堆备选名。不是我在推这个，是运营团队另一个人搞的，他搭了这产品可能的模型，但还没名字，所以先占位。占位放啥？X。于是UberX。然后公司跑得够快，产品过了绿灯、上线了，一晃十二年、十一年、whatever，UberX这个名字就定下来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is hilarious. I love it. So it was a placeholder. It's like many products start that way where they're like, this is just the temporary name, and they're like, okay, I guess everyone just knows it this way now we're going to stick with it.
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。我喜欢。所以就是个占位符。很多产品都这么开始——'这就是临时名'，然后大家说'算了，所有人都这么叫了，就保留吧'。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Exactly. It's too expensive to change and rebrand at this point.
turns.zh: 对。到这时候再改名、再品牌化，代价太大了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome story.
turns.zh: 这故事绝了。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: One that is good about scaling Uber uberPOOL in China is we were launching Uber pool in China and this was going to be, China at the time was pretty big for Uber, but uberPOOL was not there yet, and so we were going to launch. And myself and a few other folks were in Chengdu China, which is the first Chinese market that we were launching uberPOOL in and we were going to be on the ground took to launch. We wanted to go live at, I believe it was 6:00 AM for rush hour on, I don't remember the day, but whatever, Monday morning, and so we're there over the weekend getting ready to set up and at the same time we were doing some data center testing. And so we flipped on all the testing infrastructure and thought it was going to work and nothing works, and the matching algorithm just isn't working and we're like, oh my god, now it's whatever, 5:00 PM the day before we're supposed to go live, 6:00 PM, 7:00 PM okay, let's get on the phone with the US, try and figure out what's going on. (00:14:43): I remember I slept about 30 minutes that night between 2:00 and 3:00 AM being like, okay, well, we have to go live at 6:00 AM I think there was some press around it. We were planning on going live and I think we got everything finally working at probably about five 30 or six in the morning and launched just in the nick of time. And I'll never forget, we launched, it was great, we monitored, everything was good, and then we walked out for breakfast at 7:30 in the morning. Everyone sleep depressed, no one slept all night and we got these pancakes street food things and I have to imagine they were not that good, but in my mind it was the best meal I've ever had in my life.
turns.zh: 另一个关于在中国 scaling uberPOOL的：我们要在中国上线uberPOOL。中国当时对Uber挺重要，但uberPOOL还没进。所以我们准备上线。我和另外几个人在中国成都——这是我们要上uberPOOL的第一个中国市场——要在现场盯着上线。我们想在早高峰，我记得是早上6点，周几我忘了，总之周一早上。所以我们周末就在那准备、搭环境，同时还在做数据中心测试。结果我们把所有测试设施一打开，以为能跑，啥都不行，匹配算法就是不动。我们当时想'我的天，明天就要上线了，现在大概是发布前一天下午5点、6点、7点，行吧，赶紧打电话给美国，搞清怎么回事'。（00:14:43）我记得那晚我大概只在凌晨2点到3点之间睡了半小时，心想'咱6点得上啊'，而且好像还有媒体盯着。我们计划上线，最后大概是早上5点半到6点全搞定了，卡着点上线。我永远忘不了：上线了，很顺，我们盯着，一切都好，然后早上7点半出去吃早饭。所有人困得不行，一晚没睡，我们买了那种街边煎饼类的东西，我猜味道一般，但在我脑子里那是我这辈子吃过最好的一顿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like a meal after a marathon or a big hike.
turns.zh: 就像跑完马拉松或长途徒步后的一餐。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everything's so delicious. This comes up a lot of just these moments that are so incredibly stressful and hard and leap deprived end up being the best memories and the best stories to tell and things you look back at fondly. It's so weird how human nature is like that.
turns.zh: 什么都好吃。这种事老出现——那些极度高压、艰难、缺觉的时刻，到头来却成了最好的回忆、最好的故事，让人怀念。人性真是怪成这样。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, I mean another one more recent for Opendoor was when COVID hit, physically we buy and sell homes, and so we were physically going into people's homes and suddenly March 2020 going into people's homes was not something people were comfortable with. And you look at the real estate data coming out of China at the time and it looked like coming to a standstill, and so we actually turned off the core business and we stopped buying homes for a few months. hey, we can't go in and we don't know if anyone's going to be buying any homes, and so what do we do? And we took those few months and then came out the other side and had virtualized the whole process. Then it was pretty stressful, right, because looking at a business that relies on going into people's homes and suddenly you can't do that anymore, what do you do? So, again, a fond memory to look back on a very stressful time in the moment where it feels very, very difficult.
turns.zh: 对，再说个近点的，Opendoor是COVID那次。我们是真买卖房子的，得进人家家里，突然2020年3月，进别人家这件事大家都不舒服了。你看当时中国的房地产数据，基本停摆。于是我们真把核心业务关了，停了几个月不买房子——'咱进不去，也不知道还有没有人买，咋办？'我们利用那几个月，从另一头出来时，已经把整个流程虚拟化掉了。那段时间挺压迫的，对吧？一个依赖进别人家的生意，突然进不去了，你怎么办？所以回看，那是很困难时刻里一段珍贵的记忆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just since you mentioned Opendoor, I think many people have heard of Opendoor. Maybe just give a quick explanation of what Opendoor does for people that aren't exactly sure.
turns.zh: 既然提到Opendoor，我想很多人听过。给不太确定的人快速解释下Opendoor是干啥的？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: So we're a digital platform to buy and sell real estate. The core product today is a seller focused product where people can go online, enter some information about their home, and we'll make an all cash offer to be able to sell simplicity and certainty. So the product really works for people who want something that is certain and simple and easy. I don't know if you've ever sold a home, but it can be a very, very, very successful difficult process with showings and open houses and how to price it and will it sell and all of that stuff. And so we offer basically a way to skip the whole process.
turns.zh: 我们是个买卖房产的数字平台。今天的核心产品是面向卖家的：人们上线、填点房子信息，我们就给一个全现金报价，换来简单和确定。所以这个产品真正服务的是那些想要'确定、简单、省事'的人。你卖过房就知道，那过程可能非常非常难——看房、开放日、怎么定价、卖不卖得掉，全都是事。而我们基本是给你一条跳过整个流程的路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you basically sell your house to Opendoor and it's just like, cool, done, move on.
turns.zh: 所以你基本就是把房子卖给Opendoor，然后'好了，搞定，走人'？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: You picked your closing date, you move out when you want. Yeah, there's no hassle.
turns.zh: 你选个过户日期，想什么时候搬就什么时候搬。对，毫无麻烦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds amazing. I want that. Coming back to ops and product, just to close this thread again, you've worked at two businesses that have done incredibly well combining product and ops. Are there any just broad lessons you've taken away from how to make these two teams and functions work well together and to build a business that's very ops heavy but also offer driven?
turns.zh: 听着太香了。我想要。回到产品和运营，把这条线收个尾：你待过两家把产品和运营结合得极好的公司。关于怎么让这两支团队、这两个职能好好协作，建一家运营极重、但又产品驱动的公司，你有什么宽泛的教训？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: The first one we touched on, which is a, there's just got to be mutual respect. Both functions have their time and their place and their skillsets, and you just don't build big businesses of this type without respecting the fact that that both need to exist. The second, particularly on the product and engineering side, is really understanding where and how the technology leverage comes from the business and then being really focused on making sure generally, especially in the earlier days, you are more limited on the technical resourcing side than you might be on the operational resourcing side. And so how do you be really focused on where to invest your time, effort, and energy technically, which is why most of the engineering effort for Uber was on the dispatching system and the pricing system. That's just where the leverage was at the time, given the scarcity of resources. (00:19:11): And so I think the second one is being really intentional about where those techs are and then being really forthcoming and saying, hey, that means all these other places where yes, it can make things easier, more efficient, et cetera, et cetera. We are okay not investing in right now, and that needs to be an explicit decision and very transparent. But then the last bit I would say is a deep understanding that the real world has entropy and it's hard and it's messy for us at Opendoor, we go into homes, someone may not be home, scheduling may be off, at Uber the driver may cancel the radio GPS. All these things happen, right? Computers are deterministic, but humans aren't, right? And so building products that have a little bit more flex or a little bit more fail safes in case those things happen becomes a little bit more of a paramount. (00:20:08): One other thing, the last thing I would say is I think that the companies evolve as well. So what I talked about at the beginning of Uber being very focused from an engineering and product side on the dispatching system and the pricing system, obviously over time not to evolve now it centralized all of these functions as the company got bigger and more mature and scale and optimization started to be more important and expansion and that Petri dish of trying new stuff and the tools got better and the tech got easier and there was more internal infrastructure. And so over time things can start one way and shift over time as the business needs.
turns.zh: 第一个我们聊过：必须有互相尊重。两个职能都有属于自己的时机、位置和技能，没有这种'两者都必须存在'的认知，你根本建不起这类大公司。第二，尤其在产品和工程侧，是要真懂技术和杠杆到底从生意的哪来，然后非常聚焦——尤其早期，你在技术资源上比在运营资源上更受限。所以你怎么非常聚焦地把时间、精力、能量投在技术该投的地方——这也是为什么Uber大部分工程力气都花在调度系统和定价系统上。那会儿杠杆就在那，因为资源稀缺。（00:19:11）所以第二点是：非常有意地定下技术的位置，然后非常坦率地说'嘿，这意味着其他很多地方，虽然技术能让它更容易更高效，但我们现在选择不投'——而且这必须是个显式决定、非常透明。最后一点：要深懂真实世界有熵、又难又乱。对Opendoor来说，我们进人家房子，人可能不在家、排期可能乱；对Uber，司机可能取消、GPS可能飘。这些都会发生，对吧？电脑是确定性的，人不是。所以产品要多留点弹性、多点fail-safe，以防这些事发生，这变得格外重要。（00:20:08）还有一点，最后一句：公司也在进化。所以开头我说Uber早期工程和产品非常聚焦在调度和定价系统……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually spend more time there. You keep saying things that make me want to dig deeper. So at Airbnb we went through the same thing where there was all these local ops teams driving supply, finding homes, bringing out the platform, and then there's this tipping point where the product in organic growth or word of mouth ended up driving more and then orders of magnitude more. So there was no need for these folks to spend time doing these things. Can you just maybe share an example, either we Opendoor, when you talk about there's a time and a place and a skillset for ops, how that evolved? What was the team doing initially and then what did they end up doing as things grew?
turns.zh: 我们多花点时间在这。你老说些让我想往下挖的话。Airbnb也经历过同样的：一堆本地运营团队在驱动供给、找房子、把东西搬到平台上，然后有个拐点——产品或自然增长、口碑，开始驱动得更多，然后是指数级更多。于是那些人没必要再花时间干这些了。你能举个例子吗，比如Opendoor，你说运营有它自己的时机、位置和技能，它是怎么进化的？团队一开始在干啥，长大后又在干啥？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, maybe a very easy good example to pick just one part of the Uber process in the early days is at small scale, actually back when it was Uber black drivers, every driver was individually onboarded in a 90 minute to a two-hour in-person in the office onboarding with deep setting of expectations. The next version of that... So that's obviously very ops driven. The next version of that is a small classroom type setting of three or five or six drivers at a given time. Also, very ops driven. And then as we got into more mass market products like Uber Taxi or UberX, it was like, okay, maybe 20 or 30 at a time. So now it's a little bit bigger classroom setting. And we said, okay, let's make a video. Instead of giving verbally the same presentation, let's just make an onboarding video and that was the next set of scale, but now suddenly we have a different problem, which is okay, you have to validate all of these credentials. (00:22:32): So most driver's license who they are, all that stuff at one person, easy at three to four at a time, easy, 10 at a time, a little more challenging but fine. At 20 at a time, okay, you're starting to run up onto it now you fast-forward six months and you're doing a thousand a week or whatever, suddenly your system breaks and it's like, okay, we have reached the point where operational system improvements is no longer viable. So, you say, okay, we have gone from the iteration stage to the scale stage and technology is uniquely good at scaling. So now we say, okay, instead of having a bunch of folks around the world taking pictures of driver's licenses and validating and doing all that stuff, how do we integrate with some type of OCR technology or auto recognition of driver's licenses that feeds to a system that knows what a driver's license is or can do automatic validation and suddenly you've done two things. (00:23:27): One, you've scaled your system, and two, you've just created a ton of time for what at the time was probably dozens if not hundreds of people running these onboarding sessions all over the country, the world at the time to do other stuff. And so now you can level that up and say, okay, do we do more analytics? Do we do more figure out the next process that needs optimization or whatever the case may be in that virtuous cycle just continues.
turns.zh: 好。举个早年间Uber特别好懂的例子：小规模时，还是Uber Black司机那会儿，每个司机都是一对一、在办公室做90分钟到两小时的面谈onboarding，深度对齐预期。下一版……显然很运营驱动。再下一版：三五个人、六七个人一屋的小课堂式。也很运营驱动。等我们做更大众的产品，比如Uber Taxi或UberX，就变成一次二三十人。于是是更大的课堂。然后我们说'好，咱做个视频吧'——与其口头重复同一套PPT，不如做个onboarding视频，那是下一阶的scale。但突然你有了个新问题：你得验证所有这些资质。（00:22:32）驾照是谁、身份啥的，一个人时容易，三四人时容易，十人时有点挑战但还行，二十人时你开始撞墙。快进六个月，你一周处理一千个，系统突然崩了——'好，我们到顶了，运营侧的优化已经撑不住了'。于是你说'好，我们从迭代阶段进了scale阶段，而技术天生擅长scale'。所以现在我们说'与其让全球一堆人拍驾照照片、做验证，不如接个OCR或自动识别驾照的技术，喂进一个知道什么是驾照、能做自动验证的系统'。一下子你做了两件事：（00:23:27）一，系统scale了；二，你给当时那拨人腾出大量时间……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I like to think about this is do things that don't scale and then scale the things that you're doing. That's the phrase I always come back to.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这么想：先干那些不scale的事，然后再把你正在干的事scale起来。这句老话我常回到的。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of a hot take that previous podcast guest shared in a newsletter post Casey Winters. He talked about that operations is usually, and it's a hot take, that operations is a sign of inefficiency and over time your job is to squeeze that away and make it product software as much as possible. Doesn't mean you always get there. Thoughts?
turns.zh: 这让我想起上期客Casey Winters在newsletter里的一个hot take。他说运营通常是——这是个hot take——运营是低效的标志，你的工作随着时间，就是把它挤掉、尽可能变成产品软件。不是说你总能做到。你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, I actually don't. Fundamentally, it depends on what the operations is, but I don't fundamentally disagree, but I think that the right lens to think about it is... And then those folks can move on to the next challenge. And so there's always another hill to climb. And so I think that was one of the things at Uber and Opendoor where there's this culture of on the ground experimentation that's really helpful where we were just talking about driver onboarding may now be solved with technology so you have a few extra hours a day. How do we get better at optimizing the UberX system? How do you start tinkering with food delivery? How do you start thinking about higher capacity vehicles? How do you think about better feedback loop for those manual surge pricing toggles that we talked about? So I generally agree it just generally free across and solve more problems.
turns.zh: 对，其实我不完全同意。根本上取决于这运营是什么，但我不根本反对；我觉得正确的视角是……然后那拨人能去爬下一座山。所以总有下一座山要爬。我觉得Uber和Opendoor都有这种'前线实验'的文化，特别有用——刚聊的司机onboarding也许现在被技术解决了，你每天多出几小时。那怎么把UberX系统优化得更好？怎么开始捣鼓外卖？怎么开始想大容量车？怎么想我们聊过的那些手动surge开关的更好反馈环？所以我大体同意，只是它普遍是把问题释放出来、去解更多问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like a big part of this is making sure the operations teams understand there's more opportunity, even if this ends up being automated, your job is not going to go away. We're going to find something new to try and experiment and do things that don't skip.
turns.zh: 感觉这里大头是：要让运营团队明白'还有更多机会，哪怕这事最终被自动化了，你的活也不会没'。我们会找新的东西去试、去实验、去干那些不scale的事。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Going a completely different direction.
turns.zh: 好。换个完全不同的方向。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I hear you're very good at product reviews.
turns.zh: 听说你特别擅长做产品评审（product review）。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A few people told me this. I'm curious how you set up a product review and any things you've learned, any tips for how to run an effective product review?
turns.zh: 好几个人跟我这么说。我好奇你是怎么搭一场产品评审的，学到了什么，有没有什么跑好一场有效产品评审的窍门？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: That's very whoever mentioned that. But yes, big fan of doing them actually in particular to maybe bridge the conversations in companies that have ops driven cadences or start out very ops driven because the cadences can sometimes be different. And so the operational cadences that you might have something like a WVRA weekly business review may not be conducive to always picking your head up and saying like, Hey, where's the product going on a slightly longer timeframe. And so I think product reviews in general for all companies are probably really helpful, but actually in particular for some of the product and operations led companies. In terms of things I've learned, I think being really intentional about what the goals are, I think it's okay to say that there are two goals, a goal of accountability and inform to an audience. (00:26:43): But also most importantly, I think this is the primary goal is to help make the product better, to help the teams think through a problem and to have that, again, back to our earliest conversation, be a very intellectual conversation about the work and how to make the product better and not super scary. Product reviews hopefully are not feeling like firing squads. That's a scary environment to be in and not necessarily one that's conducive to how do we make the product better. Obviously sometimes the conversations have to get a little intense, but in general that's what we're shooting for is something that helps the team go back and think through how to make the product better.
turns.zh: 谁提的我得谢谢他。不过确实，我是大粉丝，尤其对那些靠运营节奏起步、或一开始极度运营驱动的公司——因为它们的节奏有时跟产品不一样。运营侧你可能有个WBR（周业务回顾）之类的节奏，但不一定利于你抬头看'嘿，产品在稍长一点的时间线上往哪走'。所以我觉得产品评审对所有公司大概都有用，但对这些产品+运营驱动的公司尤其有用。说到学到的：我觉得要有意地定下目标是什么。可以说有两个目标——问责的目标，和向听众同步信息的目标。（00:26:43）但最重要的、我认为是主要目标的，是让产品变得更好，帮团队把问题想透；回到我们最早那次对话，是一场关于这工作、关于怎么让产品更好的、非常理性的对话，而不是吓得要死。产品评审最好别像行刑队。那环境吓人，也不利于'我们怎么把产品搞好'。当然有时候对话得激烈点，但总体上我们追求的是：帮团队回去把产品怎么改得更好想透。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the two goals you try to communicate for your product reviews, accountability slash informing people what's happening, but also just like we are here to make the product better and setting that context. Yep. Is there anything you'd do specifically to make it not feel like a firing squad? Like you're coming in here to be attacked and criticized? Do you set context at the beginning of the meeting? Is this just a part of the culture?
turns.zh: 所以你试图传达的两个目标：问责/同步大家发生了什么，但同时也是'我们是来让产品变好的'，并把这语境定下来。对。有没有什么具体做法，能让它不像行刑队——不像'你是来挨批挨攻的'？是会议一开始就定语境？还是文化的一部分？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, I think definitely part of the culture, but also I am a firm believer in general that the people closest to the problems also have the best context to solve that problem. And so as a more senior voice in the room, often the job is probing, asking questions, throwing out ideas in a way that says like, hey, this is an idea. This is not a mandate, this is a thought. And if there's context missing that would inform the product direction, then providing that context in not a question asking sense, but hey, this is context that you might not be aware of. And so I think it's all in how you show up as a leader and what that looks like in terms of probing and pushing the team on dimensions that they may not be thinking about. And then understanding that the team is bringing a perspective that you don't have, which is they think about this problem 40, 50, 60 hours a week, and you might think about this problem three hours a week. So you bring them a breath, the team brings a depth in haven't been there yet.
turns.zh: 我觉得当然是文化一部分，但我也坚信一点：离问题最近的人，也最有上下文去解那个问题。所以作为屋里更资深的声音，工作常常是' probing、问问题、抛想法'，方式是'嘿，这是个想法，不是命令，是个念头'。如果有缺失的上下文会影响产品方向，那就提供那个上下文——不是用提问的方式，而是'嘿，有个你可能不知道的上下文'。所以全看你怎么以leader身份出现、怎么去probe、怎么推团队想他们没在想的维度。同时你要明白：团队带来的视角你没带——他们一周想这问题40、50、60小时，你可能只花3小时。所以你给他们广度，他们给你深度，你还没到过那深度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you heard Dharmesh Shah's episode or his thing on flash tags. Have you seen this?
turns.zh: 不知道你听没听过Dharmesh Shah那期，或者他关于flash tags（标签）的那套？看过吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I have not, no.
turns.zh: 没看过，没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. He has a whole system. So you talked about how as a leader you want people to not take everything you tell them as feedback as I need to do this. So he has a whole set of hashtags that communicate how important this is to him from hashtag FYI to suggestion, to a plea.
turns.zh: 好。他有一整套系统。你刚说作为leader，你不想让大家把你说的每句话都当'我得照做'的反馈。所以他有一整套hashtag，传达这事对他多重要——从#FYI到#suggestion到#plea。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A plea to you.
turns.zh: plea就是恳求你。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: This was actually explained to me. I don't think I've seen the original source, so I'll go back and watch it, but this was explained to me as I'm actually a big fan. I think that's great.
turns.zh: 这个其实是别人给我解释过的。原始出处我应该没看过，我会回去看看。但别人给我解释时我就成了大粉丝。我觉得太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, just get everyone on the same page. Okay. Maybe one last question here. Who do you try to invite to product reviews? Do you have any frameworks and ways of thinking of who to invite, who not to invite?
turns.zh: 对，就是让大家对齐。好。也许这最后一个问题。你一般邀请谁参加产品评审？有没有什么框架、怎么想该邀请谁、不该邀请谁？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, good question. We, I would say have oscillated over time, but in general, big subscribers of the best conversations happen when they're relatively small, so try and keep it under 10. Could be wide distribution of the document. The artifacts created are actually really powerful and they're powerful for the whole team to understand. And secret power is they're very powerful for new people who are onboarding to be like, here are the last 20 product reviews, you'll get a pretty good idea of what's going on. But generally the conversation itself try and be relatively tight. We try to keep it under 10.
turns.zh: 好问题。我们其实随时间摇摆过，但总体上，最铁粉的看法是：最好的对话发生在人相对少的时候，所以尽量控制在10人以内。文档可以广发。产出的那些'制品'（artifacts）其实极有力量，对整个团队理解在发生什么很有用。隐藏力量是：对新onboarding的人极有用——'这是过去20场产品评审，你看完就大概懂在干啥了'。但对话本身尽量收得紧，控制在10人以内。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And these artifacts, you mean the recordings of the meeting that people can watch or?
turns.zh: 这些制品，你是指会议的录像大家能看，还是——

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah. Or just the document depends on what the company culture is, whether you want to record it or just have the document either way.
turns.zh: 对。或者就文档，看公司文化——你是要录，还是只留文档，都行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then is there some specific cadence you operate on? Is it like a weekly product review that people can sign up for? Does every team, how do you like to set this up the cadence?
turns.zh: 那节奏上有什么具体安排？是那种大家能报名的周产品评审吗？每个团队都来？你偏好怎么定节奏？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, obviously it scales are with the size of the company. For us right now, what's working well is signup cadence. We have two slots a week that anyone can sign up for as their product area needs it. And then if there's something that we would love to see that we haven't seen in a bit, we do a little bit of all in telling to make sure that the work is generally cycling through on a quarterly basis.
turns.zh: 对，显然随公司大小变。我们现在好用的是'报名制'。一周两个slot，任何团队按自己产品区域的需要来报名。如果有我们想看、但一阵子没看到的，我们会稍微'推一把'，确保工作在季度内大致循环过一遍。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah. I think like all frameworks, the right answer is to pick your set of frameworks, have more tools in your toolbox, and then actually understand when and how to apply them. So we try to avoid being a hammer and everything's a nail. We try to for course the framework if it's not working. But I think what I really like about it is it forces you to put yourself in the customer's shoes. I think in a slightly deeper way and be a little bit more empathetic when I think about building at Opendoor versus say building at Uber or when you are building at Airbnb is we are not... Most people at Opendoor, we don't have homes to sell every week or every month, nor do we buy homes every week or every month. On average in the US is something people do once every seven years. (00:33:10): I'm sure the average at Opendoor is something similar, and so it's a little bit harder to be a customer. I took Uber every day. You probably use Airbnb a number of times a year. And so in some sense for some of those companies, you can bill for yourself, you would intuit the job to be done because you're just doing it for yourself. We don't necessarily have that context. And so a framework that forces us to be really thoughtful and intentional about how a customer might perceive our product is really helpful. The other thing that I like about it is the canonical version of it encourages you to think about the context in which the user's operating or the other things outside of your product that they might be going through. (00:33:59): And in our case, the home buying or selling journey often is a certainly multi-week, if not multi-month or multi quarter journey with a lot of complexity and a lot of conversations outside of our product. You may be talking to an agent, you may be talking to a friend, you may be driving around the city trying to find a house, and the framework is very flexible and encouraging of saying what is actually the job to be done of this user when they're thinking about our product and what is the context in which they're operating.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得跟所有框架一样，正确答案就是挑你那套框架、工具箱里多几样，然后真懂什么时候、怎么用。所以我们尽量别'手里有锤，看啥都是钉'。不管用就换框架。但我真正喜欢它的点是：它逼你站到客户鞋里。我觉得这是一种更深一点的方式，也更共情。我在想Opendoor建东西、对比在Uber或Airbnb建东西时，我们不是……Opendoor大多数人，不是每周每月都有房子要卖，也不是每周每月都买房。美国平均大概是七年一次。（00:33:10）我猜Opendoor的平均也差不多。所以'当客户'对我们难一点。我每天坐Uber，你一年用几次Airbnb。所以对有些公司，你能替自己bill——你直觉上就知道待办任务是啥，因为你自己在干。我们不一定有那上下文。所以一个逼我们认真、有意地去想'客户会怎么看我们的产品'的框架，极有用。另一点我喜欢的是：它的经典版本鼓励你想'用户运作的上下文'，以及你产品之外他们可能在经历的事。（00:33:59）对我们，买房卖房之旅通常是好几周、甚至好几个月、好几个季度的旅程，极复杂，大量对话发生在我们产品之外——你可能跟中介聊、跟朋友聊、开车满城找房子。这框架很灵活，也鼓励你说'当用户想着……时，他真正的待办任务到底是啥'……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to go one level deeper to talk about how you actually implement it. Do you have templates of, you have a startup project as a blank, I blank, blank, blank? How do you...
turns.zh: 我想再深一层，聊你怎么真正落地它。你们有模板吗，比如'你有个启动项目，作为空白，我空白、空白、空白'？你们怎么……

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I would say we're medium rigorous on template standardization or adherence. So we do have a template, the standard product review template talks about jobs to be done and has a section for what is the problem statement and what are the jobs to be done.
turns.zh: 我会说我们在模板标准化/遵循上是'中等严格'。我们确实有个模板，标准产品评审模板里会聊待办任务，有一段是'问题陈述是什么、待办任务是什么'。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is a doc that when you're coming to a product review, the person running it and coming is filling out this document?
turns.zh: 这是一份文档，来参加产品评审的人、主持的人，会把它填好？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Correct, pre-filling it up, sorry, pre-filling it out. And again, I think we are not sticklers about always using that template, but I think the beauty of a template is yes, it sets expectations of what you expect, but it's also just easier often for people to be able to work off something. And so yeah, it's part of our product review template and then part of our planning process as well. Because we've used it for a while. I think there's been an internalization of the culture where people will also just start commenting about it or writing about it and saying, hey, what is the job to be done here? Or what is the user trying to do? Which is maybe another colloquial phrase in it. And so, yeah, I think there's a cultural seeping that has happened.
turns.zh: 对，提前填好——抱歉，是提前填。再说一遍，我们不是死守这模板，但模板的美在于：它设了你对内容的预期，而且大家照着东西写也更容易。所以它既是我们产品评审模板的一部分，也是我们规划流程的一部分。因为用了一阵子，文化里有了内化——人们会自发评论、写'嘿，这的待办任务是啥'或'这用户想干啥'，也许是另一种通俗说法。所以有一种文化渗透发生了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: From memory, just what is in this template. So what's the phrasing that you try to use for setting up a problem?
turns.zh: 凭记忆，这模板里都有啥。你一般用什么措辞来设定一个问题？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I mean, the specific framing, I would have to go remind myself on the template itself, but generally it looks like context, problem, potential solution, risks, risks/premortal and measurement of success. And then we also try to bucket our product reviews by stage. So you could be in the ideation stage, which might look very different than at the very end of the process. Like, Hey, we're getting ready to ship speak now forever hold your piece. Those two artifacts will also be very different.
turns.zh: 对，对。具体框架我得回去对着模板提醒自己，但大体是：上下文、问题、潜在方案、风险（风险/事前复盘）、成功度量。然后我们也按阶段给产品评审分桶。你可能处在构思阶段，那跟流程最末端'嘿我们要发了，现在不说永远别说了'长得很不一样。那两份制品也会很不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So it's not as a blank the standard jobs to be done language, it's not exactly how you implement it's more just make sure we're thinking of it what is the problem for the customer? What is the context of their problem?
turns.zh: 好。所以不是那种空白的、标准的待办任务句式，不是精确怎么落地，而是'确保我们在想：对客户的问题是什么、问题的上下文是什么'。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Correct. Yeah. Yeah, we're not math living our template.
turns.zh: 对。对，我们不是被模板绑死。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. Any other tips or lessons about just working well with this concept of jobs to be done? Maybe when you come into Opendoor and like, hey everyone, we're going to be thinking this way. Is there anything there that would be useful to people if they're trying to operate this way?
turns.zh: 好，棒。关于跟'待办任务'这个概念好好协作，还有别的窍门或教训吗？比如你刚进Opendoor说'嘿大家，我们要这么思考'。如果有人想这么运作，那里有没有什么有用的？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Recognizing that correctly implementing a framework, any framework, but if you don't in particular, we can talk about takes a little bit of time and getting used to and understanding. And so I don't think you can just like, okay, we're going to make the template and then that makes the content better. That just takes people's content and they wedge it into the template. It's actually the cultural internalization of like, hey, this might be phrased as the job to be done, but is this actually the job to be done? Let's talk about why the customer might be in that situation or not be in that situation. Or I think the job to be done might actually be something else. (00:37:43): Or you might say, hey, the job to be done is maybe an early day version would be the job to be done is to get an offer from Opendoor. And it's like, well kind of, but the broader job to be done might be price discovery for the customer. And so you can have a rich conversation where it's like, well, one might be a little bit influenced by our business goals. I don't think you just run around and people are like, yeah, I'm going to sell my house, but my goal is to get an offer from Opendoor. And so that's like, okay, the template might be the same, but it's actually the content that takes a little bit of cultural instantiation.
turns.zh: 要认识到：正确落地一个框架——任何框架——都需要一点时间和适应、理解。所以我觉得你不能'好，我们做模板，然后内容就好了'。那只是把人的内容塞进模板。真正是文化的内化——'嘿，这也许被说成待办任务，但它真的是待办任务吗？我们聊聊客户为什么会在那种处境、或不在那种处境'。或者'我觉得待办任务其实可能是别的'。（00:37:43）或者你会说'嘿，待办任务可能早期版本是：从Opendoor拿到一个offer。算是吧，但更宽的待办任务可能是客户的'价格发现'。所以你能有一场丰富的对话——'一个可能受了点我们业务目标的影响'。你不会跑出去别人就说'对，我要卖房，但我的目标是拿Opendoor的offer'。所以模板可能一样，但真正是内容需要一点文化上的落地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And it sounds like people talk from what is the job to be done that feels like a core part of the way you think about it. What is the job to be done? Just that language alone feels really powerful. Is there a resource or a book that you point people to help your team learn about the jobs to be done work? Is there one thing you find useful?
turns.zh: 明白了。而且听起来大家聊'待办任务是什么'，那像是你们思考方式的核心部分。光这语言就很有力。有没有什么资源或书，你指给团队去学待办任务的？有没有一个你觉得有用的？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Not about jobs to be done. I do a lot more pointing people towards internal examples of where I saw other PMs maybe do as well or blogs and stuff. But your blog is a column when we pass around, not about jobs to done, but just about many topics.
turns.zh: 待办任务方面没有。我更多是指人们去看内部例子——我见过其他PM干得好的地方，或者博客之类。但你的博客是我们传阅的一个栏目，不只是待办任务，是很多话题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm flattered. Thank you.
turns.zh: 受宠若惊。谢谢。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really appreciate that. I was also thinking as you were talking, you're friends with Kayvon and jobs to be done on Twitter was quite the journey for them, traumatic for a lot of people. I think it went very far to the extreme of the-
turns.zh: 我真的很感激。你聊的时候我也在想，你和Kayvon是朋友，待办任务在Twitter上对他们那是一段相当折腾的旅程，对很多人挺创伤的。我觉得它走到极端了——

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah. I think they're more dogmatic about it.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得他们更教条了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very dramatic. And so I guess it's a lesson here, maybe don't take it that far.
turns.zh: 非常戏剧化。所以也许教训是：别走到那么远。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah. And I think it probably, and I don't know if Kayvon would agree with this, I imagine he would, the generalized version of you pick the right framework for the right job and if you say there's one framework to rule them all and this is the only framework that works and then of course every problem into it, then we chop.
turns.zh: 对。而且我觉得——不知道Kayvon同不同意，我猜他会——普适版是：你为对的活挑对的框架；如果你说'有一个框架统治一切、只有它管用'，然后硬把每个问题塞进去，那我们就完了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I think about jobs to be done is exactly the way you're describing it where it's just think from the lens of the job to be done for our customers. So for my newsletter, what is the job to be done of my newsletter to help you become better at your job as a product person building product. And that actually ends up being really helpful. And it feels like that's the way you guys think about it at opening.
turns.zh: 我对待办任务的理解，恰好就是你描述的那样——就是从'我们客户的待办任务'这个镜头去想。比如我的newsletter，它的待办任务是啥？是帮你作为产品人、建产品时变得更厉害。这其实极有用。而且听起来你们在Opendoor就是这么想的。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And you're crushing it by the way.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。顺便你做得 crushing it。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you. So are you. You talked about, I'm going to go into another question to deflect your compliment. You mentioned that Uber, there's a million transactions happening every second, it's massive scale. Opendoor is completely different. You have very few very large transactions. Yeah. I'm curious how you do experiments, if you do experiments, do you do A/B tests? What have you learned about just how to think through low sample sizes plus A/B testing?
turns.zh: 谢谢。你也是。你聊到……我转个问题躲开你的夸。你提到Uber每秒百万级交易、超大scale；Opendoor完全相反，是极少数的超大交易。对，我好奇你们怎么做实验、做不做、做A/B测试吗？关于小样本加A/B测试，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, very hot topic of conversation. We do A/B test. It is obviously the gold standard. And so we do as much as we can. Of A/B testing there are parts of our funnel and flow that have more volume than others. So top of quality testing easier than down funnels, A/B testing purely product or tech features easier than A/B testing processes, operational processes. But you're totally right. We are not doing hundreds of millions of transactions a year. And so experimentation can be more challenging. And so I think one way to think about it is A, acknowledge the problem, which just to say don't, and we've made this mistake many, many times, but don't just force yourself into A/B testing without running the power analysis and say like, hey, are we going to get results? What is the size that will detect and what is the runtime of that experiment? (00:41:39): And be honest, is that acceptable? A second lesson here, is there certain experiments that are important enough and it's hard to triangulate signal in any other way that you may say a six-month runtime is an acceptable outcome and we are going to start it in June and we will be smarter for it for 2025 planning and we're going to set it and forget it and we're grateful we did, and that's okay. But the only mistake here is thinking you'll get an answer in a month when you won't, and then pretending you do and then waking up a month later and being like, "Well, it was insignificant and this and that." We could have known that. And then the third thing is, and experimentation is all about increasing your conviction in the problem or the solution. So the generalized version of the statement is, if there are parts of your funnel or flow that are low end and you can't run a canonical A/B test, how might you otherwise increase your conviction in the solution that you're building? (00:42:47): And there turns out there are a decent number of other ways to do that. The first best, most obvious is talk to more customers. But there are other statistical techniques that again, aren't as rigorous or good, but may be possible. You may be able to use observational data, you review with diff and diff, you may be able to look at sister cities or twin cities. You may be able to segment by geo, you may be able to reduce your power and say, hey, we're going to run at 80% confidence for all of our experiments instead of this traditional 95% because that's a worthy trade-off. And if we're wrong one more time out of 10, that's okay. (00:43:28): You can do a long-term holdout to match your intuition. And so there's a lot of other techniques to hone your intuition. There's a lot of other techniques to build conviction and confidence. And so we try to be very creative on doing that. And then the last bit I would say is if you're not going to get significance, if there's no other techniques at your disposal, then sometimes you just got to trust your intuition and ship it. And if that's what you believe, then that's what you believed and you shouldn't spend time trying to get false precision.
turns.zh: 对，超热的话题。我们做A/B测试，它显然是黄金标准，所以我们能做的都做。A/B测试里，漏斗和流程有些部分量比别处大。所以漏斗顶端测试比下游容易，纯产品或技术feature的A/B比运营流程的A/B容易。但你完全对：我们一年不是几亿笔交易。所以实验更难。我觉得一种思路是：一，承认这问题——别说'强行A/B'，我们犯过很多次这错——要做power analysis（功效分析），问'嘿，我们到底能不能拿到结果？要检出多大的效应、得跑多久？'（00:41:39）老实说，这能接受吗？第二条教训：有没有某些实验重要到、且很难用别的方式三角验证信号，你会说'六个月时长可以接受，我们六月启动，对2025规划我们会更聪明，设了就忘、很感激我们做了，这OK'。但唯一的错是：以为一个月能拿到答案、其实拿不到，然后假装拿到了，一个月后醒来'嗯，不显著，blah blah'。这本可以预先知道。第三条：实验全是为了增强你对问题或方案的conviction（确信度）。所以普适版是：如果你的漏斗或流程某部分量低、跑不了标准A/B，那你还能怎么增强对正在建的方案的确信度？（00:42:47）结果还真有不少别的办法。第一好、最明显的是：多跟客户聊。但……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to spend more time on that last point, but real quick, the power analysis you talked about, there's people, don't know, there's calculators out there that you could just plug in, here's how much traffic I'm getting, here's how much of an impact difference I want to see, here's how long it'll take to find out.
turns.zh: 我想在那最后一点多待会儿，但快速插一句：你说的power analysis，很多人不知道，网上有计算器，你直接填——'我多少流量、想看多大的差异、要多久能知道'。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yep, exactly. Totally. And some of the calculators are great where you can also plug in the traffic and your acceptable runtime and it will tell you the minimum detectable impact and then you can gut check your own intuition. So you can play around with that.
turns.zh: 对，完全对。有些计算器很棒，你也能填流量和可接受时长，它告诉你最小可检出的效应，然后你可以用直觉gut check。所以可以玩。

turns.en: Awesome. We'll try to link to one of those in the show notes. So, on the intuition piece, is there anything more there? turns.zh: 好。我们尽量在shownotes里放一个链接。说到直觉，还有更多吗？就是你带产品团队时，怎么建议人们用直觉、或别用。因为有些公司说'我们就信数据，我不太信你意见，你又不全懂这客户'。你说过Opendoor，我自己不买房，所以我不知道能多信我的直觉。你对产品团队的一般建议是：怎么看待自己的直觉、什么时候依赖、什么时候不？

turns.zh: 对，肯定压抑。总的来说我们尽量做到：不管Zillow还是谁，要有竞争意识，但不必有竞争焦点。现实是，我们这领域空间大得很。绝大多数人还是用传统方式搬家卖房。所以这不是那种'奖品小得不够抢'的情况。现实是：这是美国最大的资产类别，只要我们死死聚焦'嘿，我们天天聊的那些客户是谁、我们服务得特别好'，不管竞争环境如何，都会生出点自信——因为市场远没饱和。（00:51:40）Uber年代也一样：交通几乎无限大。所以当年Uber和Lyft之间好像打得火热，但现实是还有大量行程在发生、人们用各种方式出行，既不全是Uber也不全是Lyft。聚焦你怎么为客户开发，才是最好的聚焦方式。

turns.zh: 我觉得这点可能在Uber早期被磨出来了。那时一切都像救火演习。所以唯一的运转方式就是……但我觉得你在问题里几乎一针见血了——带点理性地看：当你把压力反射给团队，所有人都会绷紧。反直觉的是，这不会带来更好的结果。所以另一件要在这些时刻提醒自己的事，是一堆有用的mantra（口头禅）：你从没自己想的那么好，也从没自己想的那么糟。所以那种更平稳的demeanor，能让你在压力下头脑更清、想得更明。（00:54:14）也许最没用、但不幸是现实的一个答案是：你得亲身经历些高压处境，才能有'往事会过去'的视角。而保持冷静才要紧。所以那的建议也许是：这种处境发生时，去经历它、别逃，然后从中学，下次再来时你能说'嘿，我来过这'。我在中国睡过地板、为了uberPOOL上线、以为要错过deadline。那时我工具箱里什么帮我搞定了、什么教训，我都用过。

turns.en: We'll make it through. Okay. I have this note here that I think either someone mentioned about you or you may have mentioned that product is finding the kernel of truth in a sea of ambiguity and signals. Does that mean anything to you?
turns.zh: 我们能挺过去。好。我这儿有条笔记，说要么别人提过你、要么你自己提过：产品是在一片模糊和信号之海里，找到那颗真理的内核。这对你有啥意义吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, I think in most organizations and to do the job effectively, you're going to get signals from everywhere and good ideas come from everywhere. It may be your CS team or CX team. It may be a customer directly. It may be a conversation you had. It may be a YouTube video you watched that sparked an idea. It may be feedback from an executive, it may be whatever. You went out and did a field visit. You are going to get a lot of inputs around what people think about your product, what people think you should do next. And I think that the core job is to understand what really matters, right? What is noise? What is a good idea, what is a suggestion and what is back to the jobs to be done for what is really going to move the customer forward? (00:57:24): And unfortunately that means saying no to maybe what sounds like some good ideas along the way, but if you can really figure out this is really what matters, that's the core part of the job. It dovetails even back to our earlier conversation. In the early days of building tech and ops companies is where's the tech leverage? Same question, where's the kernel of what really matters that tech can uniquely solve? And let's go do that and be comfortable with other fires maybe burning. That's what really, really, really matters. It's a hard discipline.
turns.zh: 有，绝对。我觉得在大多数组织里，要把这活干好，信号从哪来、好点子从哪来，都是四面八方。可能是你的CS或CX团队，可能是客户直接，可能是你聊过的一句，可能是你看的YouTube视频激出的灵感，可能是高管反馈，whatever——你去做了一趟field visit。关于'人家觉得你产品咋样、觉得你下一步该干啥'，你会收到大量输入。而核心的活是搞清什么真的重要，对吧？啥是噪音？啥是好点子、啥是建议、啥又是回到待办任务——什么才真能把客户往前推？（00:57:24）而不幸的是，这意味着你可能对路上一些听起来不错的点子说'不'；但如果你真能搞清'这才是真重要的'，那就是这活的核心。它甚至接回我们最早的对话：建技术+运营公司早期，'技术的杠杆在哪'？同一问题——'真正重要的那颗内核、技术能独特解决的是什么'在哪？去干那个，并舒服地让别的火先烧着。这才是真·真·真重要的。这是门难的纪律。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. If there's not an example, that's totally fine, but when you talk about this finding this kernel where tech could be highly leveraged, is there any example that comes to mind of that working out really well?
turns.zh: 我喜欢。如果没有例子完全OK，但你聊'找到技术能高杠杆的那颗内核'时，有没有哪个例子一下冒出来、做得特别好？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I mean, I think back in the Uber days, I think it was like, hey, we're not going to build sophisticated tooling infrastructure. We're not going to build a centralized growth team. We're not going to build any of that. Because if you think about the early Uber network from the simplest form, you've got a rider and a driver and you need to connect them, price the transaction and issue some receipts probably and collect payment. So it's like, okay, do we do that really well? And until we do that really well, all the other stuff is noise. It's immaterial how efficiently we answer support tickets. That's not critical. And so now it's super critical, but in the early days it's not that critical. And even the customer acquisition costs may not be super critical, in this case it's growing rapidly on the things. And so pouring fuel on the fire may not be super efficient there. (00:59:13): So I think that's a very good generalized example. One other tip that maybe is helpful that I frankly constantly work on and try to get better at is all these ideas and feedback that comes from everywhere, make sure it's written down for a number of reasons. One, you can then go reference it, but two, part of the job is making sure the people who present those ideas are heard and respected and know that it's at least somewhere where it was considered. And then you can look at it all and say, okay, but what actually really, really, really, really matters here? And yeah, that's another tip.
turns.zh: 我想回Uber早期，大概是'嘿，我们不建复杂的工具基础设施，不建集中的增长团队，那些都不建'。因为最简形式的早期Uber网络：一个乘客、一个司机，你需要把他们连上、给交易定价、出个收据、收个款。所以就是'好，我们把这干到极好？'在这之前，其他全是噪音。我们回支持工单的效率多高，都不关键。现在它超关键，但早期不。甚至获客成本早期可能也不超关键——这case里它在飞速涨。所以往火上浇油在那未必高效。（00:59:13）所以我觉得这是个很好的普适例子。另一个我老实说一直在练、想变好的tip：所有这些从四面八方来的点子和反馈，一定要写下来，原因有几个。一，你能回去查；二，这活的一部分是确保提这些点子的人被听到、被尊重、知道它至少被考虑过。然后你看着全部，说'好，但这里到底真·真·真·真重要的是什么'。这是另一tip。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say written down, is there tools you find really helpful here? Is it just put it in a big doc that we're keeping? Is there anything you find to actually operationalize that?
turns.zh: 你说写下来，有没有什么特别好用的工具？就是丢进一个大doc我们留着？你发现什么能真正把它落地？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I've seen different companies do it differently, but wherever you tend to try and keep a backlog, whether that's a Google sheet or your actual backlog in Jira, whatever you use, but at least it feels like, okay, the context was captured, and the idea is there.
turns.zh: 不同公司做法不同，但无论你习惯把backlog放哪——Google sheet也好、Jira里真正的backlog也好、whatever——至少感觉'上下文被抓到了、点子在那'。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. I'm going to take us to a recurring segment on this podcast called Failure Corner.
turns.zh: 好。好。我带大家进入这播客的常驻环节：失败角（Failure Corner）。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story you can share of a time you failed in your career had a big failure, and how that experience made you better?
turns.zh: 有没有个你职业生涯里搞砸了、大失败的故事，以及那经历怎么让你变好了？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: We can talk about the very early days of uberPOOL, and the first launch, if you will in San Francisco. So, carpooling product, multiple riders in a Mercedes car. And we had this idea that it would be effective for commuters, this was very, very early days. And so part of the launch was, okay, we're going to beta it with just some popular commuting corridors with specific companies or maybe the marina to Google or whatever and try and match people according to what their companies and that's how we'll drive liquidity. And we very quickly realized that back to what the kernel of truth is here is liquidity is the only thing that matters. And there just wasn't enough. There was never going to be enough to do this company based thing. That wasn't the strategy that was going towards from us. And so the reason I don't know if it's a full failure is maybe this is true all failures, you learn from it, you pivot and you go on to the next thing. (01:01:52): And obviously we did that and then spent a lot of our time and effort trying to say, okay, what are the bounds of liquidity and driving liquidity that we can do to understand what the most important or what the limits of the product are. So as an example, we launched and maybe people in San Francisco. Remember this $5 anywhere in San Francisco, we work for promotion, which is obviously a great deal, obviously costs a lot of money, but the whole idea here is like, oh, okay, if liquidity is what really matters, if we were to juice that and really drive liquidity, how high can our metrics get? And then we can go chase more sustainable ways to do that. But it was a interesting fail case from launching and learning to say, hey, this initial strategy just isn't going to work, we got to go. And any part of it was a hedging strategy where with a small audience and there'll be a beta population, it's like, well, this one you just got to go.
turns.zh: 我们聊聊uberPOOL最早、旧金山那次首发。拼车产品，一辆奔驰里多个乘客。我们当时有个想法：它对通勤者有效，非常早期。所以首发的一部分是：我们用几条热门通勤走廊、对接特定公司——比如Marina到Google——按公司匹配人来制造流动性。我们很快意识到，回到那颗真理内核：流动性才是唯一重要的。而根本不够。靠'按公司来'永远凑不够，那也不是我们之后要走的战略。所以我不确定这算不算完整失败——也许所有失败都这样——你学到了、转型了、去下一桩事。（01:01:52）显然我们这么做了，然后花大量时间精力去想'流动性的边界在哪、怎么驱动流动性'，去理解产品的极限在哪。比如我们上了——旧金山的朋友可能记得——'旧金山内5美元随便跑'的促销，那显然是笔好deal、显然烧钱，但整个想法是'哦，如果流动性才是真重要的，那我们给它打鸡血、真把流动性轰起来，指标能冲多高？'然后我们去追更可持续的方式。但这是个有趣的失败案例：上线、学到'嘿，这初始战略就是不行，得走'。它有点像对冲策略——小受众、beta人群，你就得直接走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think a lesson there is also don't overthink it, don't try to get too cute. Just like we're trying to make a perfect beta test versus realizing, okay, we just need a lot more people in it. Also, your $5 promotion made me think of the early promotions of the ice cream and the bunnies delivery and all that stuff.
turns.zh: 我觉得那的教训也是：别想太多、别太耍小聪明。别纠结'搞个完美的beta测试'，而是意识到'好吧，我们就需要多得多的人进来'。而且你那5美元促销让我想起早期的冰淇淋配送、兔子配送那些促销。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah. That was by the way, a example of fully distributed, the benefit of having those early Petri dishes. Someone a local marketing manager like, Hey, this would be fun. Yeah, that would be really fun. The platform can support it. And those promotions were fantastic. And it started out, I can't remember if the first one was ice cream or puppies, I think it was ice cream. But yeah, branched into all sorts of stuff. Boats, ice cream, puppies, kittens, I think, and all credit goes to local ideas of inspiration just being focused on trying to grow within.
turns.zh: 对。顺便，那是个完全分布式的例子，说明那些早期'培养皿'的好处。某个本地市场经理说'嘿，这个好玩'，'对，真好玩，平台撑得住'。那些促销棒极了。开头我忘了是冰淇淋还是小狗，好像是冰淇淋。但后来枝繁叶茂——船、冰淇淋、小狗、小猫，我想都有——全都归功于本地灵感，聚焦在'在内部生长'。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that we've circled back to the beginning of our conversation, product and ops working together, the benefits of both. Before we get to a very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you wanted to share? Any last nuggets of wisdom that you think might be useful to people when they're trying to build product companies teams?
turns.zh: 我喜欢我们绕回了一开始：产品和运营一起工作、两者的好处。在进入超刺激的快问快答之前，还有啥想分享的？关于建产品公司、团队，有没有最后的智慧金句？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: This was great. We covered quite a bit of ground. I think the only, I don't know if this is a generalized wisdom, but something I've been thinking about as my career has progressed a little bit, especially building out proper organizations, especially as more tools come online, it's very clear that there's different types of PMs and we spent a lot of time talking about once we can operate in the physical and the digital or the product and operations worlds. But even within that, there's more technical PMs who grew up in minute engineering discipline. There are people who came from ops and there are people who came from design and grew up in a more user experience background. (01:05:01): And one thing that I've been moved on as is build out the team is thinking similar to a product roadmap is it's not really about is this person good or bad or whatever, it's is this person's skillset and context to the problem that is really needed. And so back to that conversation on, hey, where do we get tech leverage? It's like, Hey, is this person who has this unique skillset as a PM for this problem type? I don't know if that's helpful, but it's something I've been spending a lot of time thinking about, especially this view job posting niche view product manager. Or it's actually like, well, how can we be a little bit more thoughtful about what the actual skillset needs off this type of team?
turns.zh: 这期很棒，覆盖挺广。我不知道这是不是普适智慧，但我职业生涯推进、尤其在建正规组织、尤其更多工具上线后，有点在想：PM有不同类型，这点很清楚。我们聊了很多'能在物理和数字、或产品和运营世界里运作'。但即便在那之内，有更技术的PM（从工程纪律里长出来），有从运营来的，有从设计来、长在本体用户体验背景的。（01:05:01）我越来越被触动的一点是：建团队时，像想产品路线图一样想——不是'这人好不好'，而是'这人的技能组和问题的上下文，是不是真需要'。所以回到那次对话'嘿，技术杠杆在哪'——'嘿，这个有独特技能的PM，适合这类问题吗？'不知道有没有用，但我花很多时间在想这个，尤其现在招PM的岗位越来越细分。或者说，我们能不能对'这类团队到底需要什么技能'想得更周到点？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. It's like a person product fit.
turns.zh: 好。这就像'人岗契合'（person-product fit）。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 说得好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think it's because a lot of companies hire generalists and they're just like, we'll hire someone smart, ambitious, and with experience and general experience and then we'll put them on different things. So I think these are two different philosophies and it probably makes a lot of sense for an Opendoor with very unique type of business, with very specific skills that are necessary to be really good there. Okay, amazing. Brian, with this, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我觉得是因为很多公司招通才，'我们招个聪明、有野心、有经验的人，然后放不同事上'。所以这是两种哲学，对Opendoor这种生意极独特、需要极特定技能才能干好的公司，后一种大概更有道理。好，绝了。Brian，到这我们进入超刺激的快问快答。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Let's do it. Can't wait.
turns.zh: 来吧。等不及了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 来吧。第一个问题：你最常推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Shoe dog, Black Swan, Design of Everyday Things, and for a fun one, Shawn Theron.
turns.zh: 《鞋狗》（Shoe Dog）、《黑天鹅》（Black Swan）、《设计中的设计》（Design of Everyday Things），加一本轻松的：《降临》（Arrival，原文Shawn Theron，应为电影Arrival）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Four books for the price of two to three. I love it.
turns.zh: 绝了。两三本的价格给你四本。我爱了。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Apologies. I'll stick to the rules.
turns.zh: 抱歉。我守规矩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, no, there's no rules. There are no rules.
turns.zh: 不不，没规矩。没规矩。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 这才对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 下一个问题：最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或剧集？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I like the sports docu ones on Netflix, so Full Swing, Drive to Survive, Break Points, tennis, golf, F1, all of them.
turns.zh: 我喜欢Netflix那些体育纪录片，比如《 Full Swing》、《Drive to Survive》、《Break Point》——网球、高尔夫、F1，全算。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And wasn't there that Nike documentary recently with Ben Affleck?
turns.zh: 前段时间不是还有个Ben Affleck演的Nike纪录片？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: There is, which I have not seen. So if it's good, I don't know if that's a recommendation or just an acknowledgement.
turns.zh: 有，我没看。所以如果它好，我不知道这算推荐还是只是知道有这回事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's worth watching. If you like Shoe Dog, I feel like you'd enjoy it. It was entertaining Michael Jordan, things like that. Next question, do you have a favorite product that you have recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 值得看。如果你喜欢《鞋狗》，我觉得你会喜欢。挺好看的，Michael Jordan那类。下一个问题：最近有没有特别爱、刚发现的产品？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: So we just got a puppy and we are about to have our first child. And so all of my purchases recently are puppies and children focused. My buddy gifted us the Phi collar for our dog, and so we've been really enjoying that. Another one as I'm getting busier for news and stuff is Particle, which is a great news aggravation tool, AI news tool.
turns.zh: 我们刚养了只小狗，又快有第一个孩子了。所以我最近的购买全围着小狗和孩子。我朋友送了我们Phi项圈（给狗的），我们特喜欢。另一个我越来越忙、看新闻用的：Particle，一个很棒的新闻聚合工具、AI新闻工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cavan's wife's business. I am a huge fan, actually I think it just came out of beta and now it's like a full app that anyone can download. I just actually installed it yesterday again and I love it. I get these pushes every few... I don't know, it's like a couple of times a day of just like, here's what's happening. Also, congratulations I should have said on your pending child.
turns.zh: Cavan老婆的生意。我是大粉丝，其实我觉得它刚出beta、现在是个谁都能下的完整app了。我昨天又装了，爱了。它隔几……我不知道，一天推几次，就'这是刚发生的事'。另外，该恭喜你即将到来的孩子。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Lucky for you. I have a newsletter post with all the products you should buy, it's called New Parent Gift Guide for Product Managers.
turns.zh: 你走运。我有个newsletter帖子列了所有你该买的产品，叫《给产品经理的新手爸妈礼物指南》。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Love it. I will definitely probably buy all of them.
turns.zh: 爱了。我大概会全买。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you don't already have them all. And now everyone's probably sending you their spreadsheets of all their favorite stuff there.
turns.zh: 如果你还没全有。现在大家大概都在给你发他们最爱东西的表格了。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, next question. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to share with people either in work or life?
turns.zh: 好，下一个问题。你有没有常回到、并分享给别人的人生格言？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Well, mostly just stay curious.
turns.zh: 基本就是：保持好奇（stay curious）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Stay curious. I love it. Two more questions. Who has most influenced you in the course of your career?
turns.zh: 保持好奇。爱了。还有两个问题。你职业生涯里谁影响你最大？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: One of the people who inspired me very early on in my product journey. I've been fortunate to have a number of very good mentors and obviously we talked about earlier while I was founders of books or me a lot from other people's journey. But one person who was personally important to me early in my product journey and very supportive of this guy named Jeff Holden, who was the chief product officer at Uber back in the day, and is like a young PM transferring into product really took me under his wing. And I think I'm forever grateful for that, for Jeff, for helping grow my career, but also try to pay it forward a little bit in terms of people who are going in the career. That was really meaningful for me.
turns.zh: 很早激发我产品旅程的人之一。我很幸运有好几个好导师，而且我们早聊过，我从书、从别人旅程学到很多。但有一个人，在我产品旅程早期对我个人很重要、也很支持我——叫Jeff Holden，当年Uber的CPO。我是个年轻PM转去做产品时，他真把我带在翅膀下。我永远感激Jeff，帮我成长，也试着把这份'传下去'给那些刚起步的人。那对我极有意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question. I hear that your interview at Uber was pretty wild. Can you tell that story?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。听说你Uber的面试相当wild。能讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yeah, I can. So, long story short, I was starting a company my senior spring before graduation and we had to go our separate ways. So I hadn't done traditional recruiting ever. And my buddy called me up and was like, "Hey, we're looking for smart, hardworking people at this Uber thing. Are you interested?" And quick side note, I had actually done some very early diligence work on these taxi apps back in 2011, looking at the time was Uber Cab and Cabilis and Taxi Manage can probably names nothing these days. And so I knew what Uber was and so I said, "Yeah, sure, I would love to." And so I had the first round of interview went well, and they said, great. And at that stage is come on onsite, the full enchilada one works, and this was post-graduation and was helping out some companies but didn't have a full-time job. (01:10:51): So I said, hey, I'm pretty flexible. How about next Tuesday? I said, great. So we scheduled it and then on Friday or Saturday or over the weekend I looked, I'm like, oh, Tuesday's, July 4th. I scheduled my interview for July 4th. And so I called my buddy and I'm like, hey, I am so sorry. I don't want to make people in on July 4th. Should I cancel? Should I reach out? Everyone's accepted. Whatever you do, do not cancel your interview. Like, okay, I'll be there on July 4th. And so I went in to the office on July 4th and there was a very small handful of people there. It was actually launching that day, was launching Uber's second ever product type, which was Uber SUV. And I had this, I think it was probably five hour gauntlet interview on July 4th from noon to five and missed my July 4th barbecue. And it was quite the experience, but I think maybe set the stage for some of the early days chaos. I'm very glad I didn't cancel the interview.
turns.zh: 能。长话短说：我大四春招前在创业，后来各奔东西，所以我从没走传统招聘。我哥们打电话说'嘿，我们在Uber这摊事找聪明、肯干的人，你有兴趣吗？'插一句：其实2011年我就做过些很早期的尽调，看当时叫Uber Cab、还有Cabilis、Taxi Manage这些现在大概没人记得的名字。所以我知道Uber是啥，我说'好啊，当然'。第一轮面得不错，他们说'太好了，来onsite，全套那种'。那是毕业后，我在帮几家公司但没全职。（01:10:51）我说'嘿我挺灵活，下周二？'‘好’。排了。然后周五六或周末我一看'哦，周二是7月4号'。我把面试排到7月4号了。我打电话给我哥们'嘿太抱歉，不想让大家7月4号上班，取消？还是联系？'‘别，千万别取消，大家都接受了。不管怎样别取消。’‘好，我7月4号去。’于是7月4号我进了办公室，那里只有极少几个人。那天其实在launch Uber第二个产品类型：Uber SUV。我经历了——大概是中午到5点、五小时的' gauntlet（连环）面试'，错过了我的7月4号烧烤。那经历相当可以，但大概也给早期混乱定了调。我很高兴没取消。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And was Travis involved in that interview or is it just-
turns.zh: Travis也参与了那次面试吗，还是——

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Travis was involved in the interview. She was one of the... I think there were four or five people, and the two who were generally guiding my interview process and Travis and one other person starting that day. And part of the gauntlet interview was a simulation of the job, if you will. And so some of that was building some novels on the computers and some of it was writing potential emails to drivers and if she had the driver come in and you did chat, so I was in this room by myself typing away on the first part, which was building the model. And I hear him knock on the door and Travis comes in and he just sits down and says, "Hi, I'm Travis." I don't know who you are, but I'm Brian, and we have a 45-minute chat, or maybe it's been about half hour, 45 minutes. And clearly I'm not producing the work that I'm supposed to of the interview. (01:12:59): I'm supposed to be building this model. I'm supposed to email it back to the person who sent it to me. Clearly I've done nothing chatting with the CEO. And I hear a knock on the door and the door opens and the person sees that I'm talking to Travis, "Oh, continue, continue" and it was very good. Also, pretty intense conversation with Travis that definitely set the expectations working there.
turns.zh: Travis参与了。他是……我觉得四五个人里之一，主要引导我面试过程的是Travis和另一个当天入职的人。那连环面试有一部分是对这活的模拟。所以有些是要在电脑上建模型，有些是写潜在给司机的邮件，如果司机进来你聊天——第一部分我自己在屋敲键盘建模型。我听见敲门，Travis进来，坐下说'嗨我是Travis。'‘我不知道你是谁，但我是Brian’，我们聊了45分钟，也许半小时出头、45分钟。显然我没在生产面试该生产的活。（01:12:59）我该建这模型，该把它邮件回给发我的人。显然我光跟CEO聊，啥也没干。又听见敲门，门开，那人看见我在跟Travis聊'哦继续继续'，挺好。跟Travis那场也挺intense，确实把在那工作的预期定下来了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And clearly worked out. And Travis was happy. Is what-
turns.zh: 显然成了。Travis也高兴。是吧——

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: I hope so.
turns.zh: 希望是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... I imagine.
turns.zh: ……我猜。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Brian, thank you so much for being here. We went through everything that I was hoping to get through. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online, and is there anything you want them to check out that you might be up to? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 绝了。Brian，太感谢你来了。我想聊的都聊到了。最后两个问题。大家去哪能网上找到你，有没有什么你正在做、想让大家看的？听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Super kind. They can find me online on Twitter, LinkedIn, both just Brian Tolkin, my name. In terms of being useful, if you have a home to sell, feel free to go on to Opendoor. More importantly, if you have feedback on the product, but would love to hear it. Otherwise, any feedback on what people liked or would love to learn more about from what we chatted about would be super great. So I'd love to hear from you.
turns.zh: 太客气。他们能在Twitter、LinkedIn找到我，都就叫Brian Tolkin，我的名字。要说有用：如果你有房子要卖，欢迎上Opendoor。更重要的是，如果你对产品有反馈，我超想听。另外，关于我们聊的这些，大家喜欢啥、想多学啥，反馈都超棒。所以我很想听你的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Brian, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: Brian，非常感谢你来。

turns.speaker: Brian Tolkin
turns.en: Lenny, I really appreciate it. This was great. Bye everyone.
turns.zh: Lenny，我真的很感激。这期很棒。大家拜拜。
